extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, journal editors, and authors interested in academic publishing and mathematical paper writing (esp. combinatorics/geometry communities)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and policy proposals about mathematical journal publishing, peer review, and practical guidance for starting and writing math papers (with examples from combinatorics and geometric inequalities). Intended to guide authors, editors, and societies on producing and evaluating mathematical research and publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough technical peer review / technical checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review should include substantial technical checking; some top journals use multiple independent teams of referees to check correctness, but practice is inconsistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Annals papers studied by six (!) independent teams of referees' is given as a positive model; counterexample: some Annals papers with 'no technical check at all'. Implicit recommendation: implement stronger, possibly multiple-team, technical verification to ensure correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctions / awards as selection mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialized or non-exclusive journals can make their own selections for best papers in their areas, functioning as awards rather than exclusive publication loci.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One paper could receive multiple such awards; this would reduce pressure to publish in a single top journal and make recognition fairer. These awards act as 'best journal where the paper could be accepted' substitutes and help authors' reputations without restricting dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: arXiv-overlay / bidding publication model
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals could operate by placing bids on the best papers (which are free on arXiv), with authors accepting the best bid and the paper being linked to the journal site in an 'arXiv overlay' style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This model separates dissemination (arXiv) from selection/brand (journals), uses clear deadlines, and treats acceptance as an offer competition similar to graduate admissions. Suggested as a way to disentangle peer review from publishing venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conference system requiring prior arXiv posting and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: A competitive conference system (like CS theory conferences) could require prior arXiv posting and track 'verified' papers accepted to a central mega-journal, disentangling correctness verification from novelty/importance evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conferences could focus on emerging tools and ideas and level the playing field for underfunded researchers. They would keep track of verified papers and promote progress without replicating journal peer review burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher acceptance rates for society journals / a large middle-tier publication venue
rubrics_metrics.description: Societies (e.g., AMS) should maintain large, free, friendly but thorough publication venues with higher acceptance ratios for solid papers that don't meet top-journal thresholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: low acceptance ratios applied uniformly have negative effects on the community; public societies have a public-good role to provide accessible venues. Practical benefit: reduce unhealthy prestige pressure and allow middle-tier journals to adapt their models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full transition to electronic publishing and no artificial page limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Stop wasting paper and fully move to electronic publishing; do not limit numbers of papers or pages, and treat brevity as a feature, not a bug.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digital formats remove print-space constraints, so acceptance decisions shouldn't be driven by page budgets. Authors should nevertheless value brevity where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent and improved electronic editorial system
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve your electronic editorial system to make it more transparent to authors, referees, and editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency reduces frustration and opacity in editorial decisions; invest in better tools and workflows to show status, timelines, and review history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team-based editorial work and paid editorial support
rubrics_metrics.description: Help editors work as a team and incentivize them financially; hire paid editorial experts (e.g., pay for 20% employment) globally to run journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial work should not rely entirely on unpaid volunteer effort. Paying part-time professional staff increases responsiveness, consistency, and institutional memory across editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals dedicated to survey articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up new journals fully dedicated to survey articles, both solicited and contributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys are valuable but underpublished; dedicated venues would elevate expository work and provide authors venues distinct from research-article standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals procedure and senior-editor roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Create an appeals procedure and add a new type of senior editors who would take the job seriously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An appeals process offers recourse for disputed editorial decisions; senior editors with clear responsibilities can ensure fairer outcomes and institutional oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutionalize awards for articles and referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Institute awards for best long, short and survey articles in the journal, and for best referees, using fair input from all editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awards incentivize quality writing and reviewing, reward service, and give recognition beyond mere acceptance. Make efforts to be fair by soliciting input from the editorial board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflict of interest between helping authors and protecting journal brand
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal editors and referees face a conflict: helping authors may hurt the journal's selectivity and vice versa; disentangling correctness checking from novelty/importance evaluation can reduce this conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mega-journal focused on correctness would aim to help authors get proofs right and accepted; selection for novelty/importance can happen separately (awards, specialized journals, conferences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreword / high-level introductory paragraph for complex papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a Foreword — a paragraph or two devoted to the philosophy underlying your work or a high-level explanation of the key idea — before stating the main result, especially for complex stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the Foreword under one page; it's a place for memorable, possibly literary description that prepares the reader. Forewords can be quoted and increase reach; referees are unlikely to object if concise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose opening strategy appropriate to the paper's story
rubrics_metrics.description: If the paper's story is simple (e.g., solving a famous conjecture), 'get to the point' works; for more complicated stories, prepare the reader with context and narrative before technical statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to 'get to the point' or build a narrative; include motivational examples and broader perspectives when the subject requires it. Reference: Martin Krieger's advice 'Don't Just Begin with "Let A be an algebra..."'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorable/literary opening lines when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider putting highly literary or memorable descriptions in the Foreword/opening if they capture the philosophy or key idea; such lines may be quoted and draw attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance literary flair with clarity; avoid gratuitous stylistic flourishes that obscure mathematical content. The author lists successful opening lines used in several of his papers as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for judging importance in enumerative combinatorics
rubrics_metrics.description: In Enumerative Combinatorics, judge importance by how natural/interesting the objects are and how strong/elegant the final formula is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether you want exact counts, asymptotics, closed formulas, generating functions, etc.; clarity on the desired type of result helps frame the paper's contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two approaches to 'proof deconstruction' / valuing inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: When an interesting inequality is established, either treat it as a tool (sharpen/generalize for applications) or treat it as an object of interest (seek the 'right proof' to understand and generalize it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both approaches are valid: the first emphasizes use and applications, the second seeks deeper structural understanding. Choose approach based on goals and nature of the inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial interpretation criterion (#P)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define a combinatorial interpretation in complexity-theoretic terms: a combinatorial interpretation should be a #P object (i.e., counting solutions verifiable in polynomial time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition both clarifies what one seeks and enables negative results (showing no #P interpretation exists under complexity assumptions). Use the #P framing to ask whether a counting function has a constructive combinatorial model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic expectations about equality/stability descriptions for deep geometric inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Equality cases and stability results for deep inequalities (e.g., Alexandrov–Fenchel) may be computationally intractable or unlikely to admit simple complete descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author's results suggest equality cases of AF are 'not in PH' (under complexity assumptions), so do not expect a full, simple stability description for such inequalities in general; focus on special cases or restricted settings where tractable descriptions exist.
